doc.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

chapter: Church, energy and the state of jazz
title: Where jazz is going: money, pensions and Milt Hinton's help
summary: Jazz now makes money; Cranshaw praises his union pension, notes that young players lack places to play, and recalls Hinton getting him a date with Bing Crosby.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I want to ask you a couple of more questions here. Where is jazz going and/or where does it need to go?

It’s hard to say because now we find out that jazz can make money. Before, there was money being made we didn’t realize it, we didn’t get most of it, but you know, we wanted to play. I say now when I go in, when I used to play in the pit and do Broadway shows, I always wondered, I tell musicians, because I’m working a lot for the musician’s union, not as a representative but as a person who was plugged in to the system by no fault of mine. I got plugged into the system and now I’m getting back I get a large pension, so that if I didn’t work another day in my life I’m really very well taken care of, my wife and I. So I’m a fortunate individual. If they would have given me the money I’d have spent it. But because somebody else put it in, so trying to talk to the younger musicians about the system and the different things that they can get involved in, which most of them are not involved in. I mean the younger guys coming up, there’s nowhere for them to play. We could go and play in Birdland. We had all of these places to play, I was invited to play. I mean I think back — Milt Hinton allowed me to play with Bing Crosby. Now I was a young guy, and I walked in and Milt Hinton had more work than he could do. And at Lincoln Center, I walked in to play the bass with Bing Crosby and Bing Crosby looked and he said, “Oh, shit” you know he said, “this guy’s too young. He ain’t going to know these tunes.” He didn’t know I was older than he thought I was and I knew the material. But it was just strange for him to see this young guy. But Milt had already started to build me and to give me the experiences that he thought I needed to do. The young guys now don’t have an opportunity for those experiences. The record companies, it’s a money making situation. So if the record company takes a young guy who is promising, they start to work. I mean it’s not about the other things.
